title: How to Solve Delinquent Time Entry at Your Law Firm
summary: PointOne shows law firms how to fix delinquent time entry with same-day policies, passive capture, mid-month visibility, and pre-bill review.
body_markdown:
### AI Summary


-


Time entry loses to billable work by default, so attorneys reconstruct the week from memory instead of logging as they go.


-


That delay is costly: a one-week lag can erase up to 20% of billable time, and thin, reconstructed entries invite write-offs.


-


The fix is earlier capture — catch a vague narrative when it's written, not weeks later at pre-bill.


## Why Do Attorneys Fall Behind on Time Entry?


Time entry competes directly with billable work. Every minute an attorney spends logging hours is a minute not spent on a client matter. Entry gets pushed to the bottom of the list. Attorneys are not choosing to skip time entry. Logging time simply never feels as urgent as the work in front of them.


Most tools built for attorney time entry ask attorneys to stop, remember the work, and type it in later. The Friday ritual is one shape this takes: an attorney reconstructs the week from the sent folder, scanning emails and calendar entries to remember what happened and how long each task took.


That process is slow, and it is also inaccurate. Reconstructed entries tend to round durations, guess at start times, or drop short tasks altogether.


## What Does Delinquent Time Entry Cost the Firm?


Delinquent time entry does not stay contained to the one attorney who is behind. It moves downstream through the entire billing cycle, and the[delay itself carries a real cost](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/law_practice/resources/law-practice-magazine/2025/september-october-2025/enhancing-productivity-in-law-firms/) . A one-week delay can cost up to 20% of billable time. More than a week can push that loss past 50%. The longer an attorney waits, the less of the actual work makes it onto the bill at all.


Late time entries create a chain reaction. When entries arrive late, pre-bill review starts late. When pre-bill starts late, invoices go out late. When invoices go out late, the firm's collection cycle stretches, and cash that should already be in the bank sits in accounts receivable instead. Each step in that chain adds days, and those days compound across every matter the firm bills. Late time entries are the leading cause of[lost realization](https://pointone.com/blog/blog-law-firm-realization-rate) . Hours that never make it onto a bill are hours the firm never collects on, regardless of how good the underlying work was.


Late entries also tend to be thin entries. An attorney reconstructing a week of work from memory late on a Friday is not writing detailed,[defensible narratives](https://pointone.com/blog/how-to-craft-better-legal-bills) . They are writing whatever they can recall in the time they have left. Vague narratives like "research" or "review documents" invite scrutiny from cost-conscious clients and give billing administrators little to defend if a client pushes back. That is one direct path to[write-offs](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/law_practice/resources/law-practice-magazine/2022/time-write-downswrite-offs-dont-let-good-cake-go-waste/) .


The compounding effect lands on cash flow for whoever owns the billing calendar. The further billing slips from the date work was performed, the longer the firm waits to get paid. Forecasting revenue with confidence gets harder at every step of that delay.


## How to Fix Delinquent Time Entry: A Five-Step Process


### 1. Write a Same-Day Entry Policy With a Firm Deadline


Most firms expect attorneys to log time "regularly." A policy with no deadline, no owner and no consequence changes nothing. A real policy names a deadline, a deadline owner, and a consequence. Same-day entry is the standard to write down, with a 48-hour allowance during trial and a hard cutoff at month-end close.


### 2. Automate Time Capture


A written policy alone does not fix a capture problem. If entry still requires an attorney to stop, remember, and type, some entries will always slip through. AI timekeeping providers like PointOne address this gap.


PointOne supports[five capture modes](https://pointone.com/blog/ai-time-capture) : manual entry with AI-drafted narratives, AI timers, AI voice capture, retroactive capture, and fully automatic capture. Retroactive capture covers a missed date range, and automatic capture logs activity in the background. The goal is the same across all five: the entry should already exist by the time anyone would otherwise have to chase it.


Together the modes allow entries created on a given day to be set to auto-release that same day. Notifications go to timekeepers with unreleased entries before the day closes, so the follow-up happens without the billing team chasing anyone. Compliance runs at the entry level: every entry is checked against the rules scoped to its matter, with non-compliant entries flagged back for edits, some as warnings and some as hard blockers that stop the entry from moving forward. AI-generated entries still require an owner, but the owner now only has to confirm client, matter, and narrative before they become billable work product.


### 3. Set the Narrative Standard at Entry, Not at Pre-Bill


Waiting until pre-bill to catch a vague narrative is too late. It means rewriting entries under time pressure, days before the invoice needs to go out.


**PointOne Rules** ingests a firm's Outside Counsel Guidelines (OCGs) from PDF, DOCX, TXT, or EML files. It converts them into structured billing rules, including narrative detail requirements and block-billing prohibitions. Those rules apply automatically to every entry as it is created. Catching a thin narrative the moment an attorney writes it costs far less than catching it three weeks later.


### 4. Build In a Mid-Month Visibility Checkpoint


Finance leadership should not have to wait until day 26 to know where the firm stands on hours. A mid-month checkpoint is a scheduled review of entry rates and outstanding hours by timekeeper. It gives finance leadership time to step in while a month still remains.


**PointOne Intelligence** surfaces this kind of visibility as a standing view. Pair the checkpoint with[tracking delinquent-entry rate as a firm KPI](https://pointone.com/blog/blog-law-firm-kpis-managing-partner) so it does not disappear between month-end closes.


### 5. Pre-Bill Review as the Final Catch


Pre-bill review checks the accuracy and compliance of entries that already exist. **PointOne Review** flags[compliance issues and narrative gaps](https://pointone.com/blog/optimizing-legal-pre-bill-proforma-review) before an invoice goes out. Used this way, pre-bill catches only the stragglers that slipped through steps one through four.


## Common Mistakes When Chasing Time Entries


Firms that struggle with delinquent time entry tend to repeat the same four mistakes.


-


**Chasing harder instead of changing capture.** More reminder emails and more one-on-one nudging add follow-up work without fixing the capture method that causes the delay. If entry still depends on an attorney remembering to sit down and type, chasing stays a permanent line item on the billing calendar.


-


**Setting a monthly cadence instead of a same-day one.** A policy that asks attorneys to "catch up by month end" builds in a month-end scramble by design. The right cadence is same-day entry, matched to when the work happens.


-


**Reconstructing time retroactively with no accuracy check.** Some firms let attorneys rebuild missed weeks from memory with no cross-check against calendar or email activity. That produces entries that look complete but are inaccurate, and the inaccuracy shows up later as a write-off.


Firms that avoid these four patterns are the ones that get delinquent time entry under control, and keep it that way.

## FAQs about Delinquent Time Entry


How does a firm de-risk billing operations when only one person knows how to chase delinquent time entries?


Document the chase process, but the better fix is removing the need for it. When capture is passive, entries exist without anyone chasing them, so the process no longer depends on one person's institutional knowledge. Pair that with a written same-day policy so timekeepers know the deadline no matter who is tracking it. That protects the firm from a single point of failure, no matter who runs billing operations day to day.


Why do attorneys end up reconstructing a week of time entries from their sent folder?


Most tools ask attorneys to remember and log time after the fact, so entries pile up over the week and the reconstruction happens all at once at the end of it. Passive and automatic capture modes log time as work happens, so there is no week left to reconstruct. Retroactive capture can also rebuild a missed date range from actual activity data instead of memory alone.


Which contemporaneous capture methods work for attorneys who are rarely at a desk?


AI timers and AI voice capture log time as the work happens. Voice capture fits attorneys who spend most of the day in court or in the car and does not require sitting at a desk to enter anything.


How do other firms get mid-month visibility on hours?


They build a standing checkpoint instead of waiting for month end. PointOne Intelligence gives finance leadership a live view of entry rates and outstanding hours. A gap shows up mid-month, while there is still time to act on it.
